question.problem: At which point on the curve ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=xy$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-xy)\,j \\  & =(-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((-2y-x)\,i-(2x-y)\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ -2y-x & =0 \\ x & =-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-2y$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =xy \\ (-2y)^{2}-{y}^{2} & =(-2y)y \\ 4{y}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =-2{y}^{2} \\ 5{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $y=0,$ we get $x=0,$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$
